title: Breaking and Entering: Lael Neale's Altogether Stranger
transcript:
Lael Neale spoke with Simon from her childhood bedroom on her family's farm in Virginia, a week after returning home from a European tour behind her fourth album, Altogether Stranger (Sub Pop). Edited for length and clarity.

Simon: You've moved back to Virginia. Is that where you're calling from today?

Lael: Yeah, I'm actually in my old childhood bedroom right now.

Simon: That's so cool. Did you live in the same place your whole childhood? That was my experience. We didn't move much.

Lael: I lived somewhere else until I was eleven, and then we moved here. So I've been here since I was eleven.

Simon: Part of why I wanted to start there is that displacement, and finding your place in a world that can feel quite alien, runs through so much of your work, and Altogether Stranger explores that tension between belonging and estrangement. Before we talk about Los Angeles: what was it like growing up where you are now, and how did it shape your relationship with nature and place?

Lael: The theme of alienation has been with me for maybe my whole life. It's like the old cliché: wherever you are, there you are. Because the alienation has less to do with the place itself than with my relationship to the place. Growing up in Virginia, I felt very at home on the farm and in nature, but I felt pretty alienated from the culture and society here. I felt very different; I just didn't really fit in. And then when I found Los Angeles, I felt very connected with the people, with the culture of artists and musicians there, in a way that was almost instantaneous: I'd meet someone and we would just get along, or be friends, or at least have some kind of connection. I felt very un-alienated amongst the people there. But the place itself was what made me feel strange: being separated from the earth, in a place that's pretty much completely concrete.

Simon: That dichotomy is something you're working through in the songs. Even going back to 'I Am the River', there's that sense of flow, but also stability. The searching is important, but so is grounding yourself.

Lael: Yeah, definitely. Finding the balance between the two. A river has the flowing water, but it also has the banks that hold it, and you need both things to have balance in your life. Otherwise it can become stagnant, or it can be wild and exploding everywhere. So it's striking the balance between flow and structure, or something like that.

Simon: Focusing in on Altogether Stranger, you're documenting Los Angeles, the place, but also the relationships you formed there. You've said that LA is the case study but the world is the subject, because the record grapples with big-picture questions: consumerism, technology, community, apocalypse, and finding hope amidst it all. And when you sing a line like "all good things will come to pass", you leave it ambiguous: it could mean a hopeful new age, or destruction. What overall feeling about humanity are you working through on this record?

Lael: It vacillates day to day. Certainly what's happening in the world doesn't leave much room for hopefulness. But I actually just wrote a Substack post, which I haven't shared yet, about the necessity of hopefulness, and how nature is hopeful against all odds. On the farm here in Virginia there's a mockingbird that keeps making a nest, and she's losing her babies. A windstorm will blow the nest away, or whatever. But she keeps making a new one and having new eggs, and now there are new hatchlings out there. I was thinking about that in relationship to humanity now. No matter how tragic and destructive things are, we have to have the hope to keep going. So I feel, maybe naively, optimistic that things are actually going to change. "All good things will come to pass" is definitely meant to be a little tongue-in-cheek, joking about: which will it be? I don't really know the answer. But I tend toward hopefulness.

Simon: That resilience in nature reminds me of an image in 'Tell Me How to Be Here', where you sing about brave houses, situating an emotional quality amongst the buildings you found yourself surrounded by. Can you talk about the specific lyrics and images you ground the album in?

Lael: As you noted, it's very much an album of that city. I'm always trying to take a universal concept, maybe something big or lofty, and ground it in the mundane, because it's a way to make a new point with an old idea. The best poems, to me, are the ones that have this tiny little minute moment, or an experience the poet has, and when the reader reads it they feel like they're the only other one who's had that same experience. That's what guides me. I can't even say it's how I write. But when something comes to me and it's like that, I go: oh, that's right. You can't force it; the idea just has to pop into your head. That's the magic, when little things like that happen. It doesn't happen that often, but it's what I'm always looking for.

Simon: You've spoken about your admiration for poets like Mary Oliver and Rumi, and about centring things in the everyday to avoid getting too lofty.

Lael: Mary Oliver is who I think of immediately, because she's so brilliant at it: taking these tiny moments and creating a profound message through them.

Simon: Where did you find yourself doing that with the lyrics on this album?

Lael: The line you brought up about the brave houses was just so natural, because I was writing at the Mellotron in the window, looking out over Sunset Boulevard and the whole neighbourhood. Where I lived in Echo Park there were incessant helicopters going around, and all the little houses looked so little and vulnerable, but the house just stands there and faces it. The helicopters I think of as the police state: the government overlords surveilling us. They feel like an intimidating, violent, aggressive presence. So I was imagining all the innocent people in their innocent little houses being surveilled and annoyed by these sharks of the sky. That was a moment where I thought: this tiny little thing sums up what's happening on a broader scale in society now. And then the trash trucks coming and taking away the garbage we create, so much of it that we have to have giant garbage trucks coming through every week to clear it away. A never-ending cycle of consumption and disposal. I'm always trying to make some kind of commentary, but to do it in the most poetic and pure way possible.

Simon: On the trash and the consumerism, is 'Sleep Through the Long Night' also a reflection on some of those things?

Lael: Yeah, definitely. I was feeling pretty sad and down about all of it, so it doesn't have as much of the humour as some of the other songs. But it's also just making fun of myself.

Simon: It feels framed, maybe, as a little bit of a lullaby. Is that right?

Lael: Yeah, because I'm talking about sleeping in it. But it's kind of a lullaby for departure from this world. The long night is death, I guess. What are we going to do while we're here, in this interim state? That song is me at a point where I was feeling pretty dead in the water. When you feel like that, and then you reflect: well, it's all going to end someday, we've got to start doing something now. I don't know if you ever feel that, but it's that numb state you can get into where you don't really feel happy or sad, you don't really feel anything, and the world is just happening to you, and you're not really an actor or player in it. That's what the song is. It's funny, I don't really think about it that much until someone asks me.

Simon: To move to a song that reflects on identity as a moving target, and one that really resonates with me, 'Tell Me How to Be Here'. It feels like the permanent question: what am I supposed to be doing right now? You wrote about it beautifully on your Substack, too. What does the song mean to you, and how did it come about?

Lael: It's both a joke and serious. I feel like now everyone's trying to tell you how to be: how to live your best life, you should do this diet protocol, you should follow this. The influencer world is all about telling you how to be in the world. So the song is making fun of that, and rejecting it. But at the same time, I've even Googled "what do people do", because there is an element of: someone just tell me what to do with my life. I want to just be told, so I don't have to think about it. Tell me how to live. What's the right way to do things? It sounds a lot easier just to follow. I understand why people follow gurus, because it's hard to think for yourself and chart your own path in the world. But I would never want to live like that either. So I go back and forth. That sounds really mundane, but that was the spark of the song: grappling with the fact that I don't ever want anyone to tell me what to do, but at the same time, I do want to be told how to live right.

Simon: It captures the contradictions of ourselves very well, humorously but poignantly. We need guidance, but ultimately it should direct us inward, to listen to ourselves.

Lael: Yeah, exactly. And it was the first of all the songs from this album that I wrote. It was when I had just moved back to Los Angeles, and I was really struggling with the readjustment to living in a city, feeling very ungrounded and strange.

Simon: On that strangeness: I understand Altogether Stranger, as a title, comes from a chorus that never actually made it onto the album, but is almost the invisible spine of the record. Is that right?

Lael: Yeah. I worked on that song for so long, and it never amounted to anything. There are five or six completely different melodies and versions of it, and it just never became anything. So I feel like its whole purpose was to give me — that was beautiful, what you said. The invisible binding, is that what you said?

Simon: The spine of the book. And you've made a film that explores that feeling of being almost an extraterrestrial in your own city: the imagery of yourself as a sequin-dressed alien.

Lael: It's a mirror suit that I ordered online from some sketchy website. When I got it, I didn't even really realise what it was: a suit completely covered with shards of mirror, and I had to peel a little plastic film off every single one of them, which took me like four hours, I swear. And I was feeling terrible about all the plastic. I was like, oh my god, I'm a horrible person. But I got incredible use out of that thing. I wore it basically until it disintegrated. And the mirror suit is a whole other commentary, too, because it's an alien walking through the world, mirroring humanity back to itself. That's what I feel my role is, and maybe the role of a lot of artists: to observe the world, come to your own conclusions about it, and reflect it back to people. And I feel like the people who resonate with a particular artist's work are maybe having a similar experience of seeing the world in a similar way. That's why I feel really connected to people who connect with the music: I'm like, oh, maybe we see the world in a similar way. I feel isolated, so it makes me feel very connected when people get the music. Because it's not like I'm a pop — you know, there's not a ton of people out there.

Simon: I have to say, that's exactly how your music makes us feel: less alone, and more connected to a shared way of seeing the world. It's a tremendous gift.

Lael: Thank you.

Simon: We only have a few minutes left, and there's so much to ask. But can we pivot to the sound of the record? I've loved your description of self-imposed limitations offering tremendous creative freedom, and of your relationship with the Omnichord as your soulmate. Can you tell us about the instrument, and what you find beautiful about it?

Lael: I trained myself on guitar, and piano a tiny bit, but barely. Mostly guitar. I played that for many years. Then in 2019 I was feeling kind of burnt out with the guitar, dead in the water with writing songs, bored with the process. And a friend loaned me an Omnichord, and it immediately opened up this whole new avenue of songwriting for me. This is the limitation part: the chords are just these long droning notes. For whatever reason the strings of a guitar can be convoluted and busy, and the Omnichord is just this one note or chord, this steady drone, and it freed my voice to make melodies I'd never made before. So I think of it as having the gift of limitation. It's this tiny little machine. I've definitely explored it a lot, but it's pretty limited, and that's what I love about it. And I still haven't felt bored yet. It's been like six years now.

Simon: Your Substack, Consensual Sound, feels like a channel to explore creativity in a different way, because of course you're also a visual artist, and there are all these mediums you move across. Can you tell us about its place in your universe?

Lael: Thanks for reading. I actually saw your name when you subscribed, I think.

Simon: I love your thoughts there.

Lael: Thank you. It's actually kind of a vulnerable avenue for me. It's a little difficult, but it's what I started out doing. In college I studied literature, and a lot of journalism, essay writing, creative writing in the long form. And I found I liked writing songs so much more, because it's a limitation, and the limitation really helped me. So the Substack can be a little daunting. But I don't want to complain too much, because the whole concept of Consensual Sound came from me being like: there's music playing every single place you go now, every gas station, every coffee shop, every single space, and I'm a musician, and I hate it. I don't want it. I want the choice. And I feel the same way about smells. It started as this rant about not consenting to this and that. But then I was like, I don't want to sound like a grumpy old woman. So now I use it to share unreleased demos: songs that will probably never see the light of day anywhere else, which is fun for me, because I have so many of them. They're kind of like your children: I care about all of them, but sometimes they just don't fit in places. So I really love it, but it's also the biggest challenge. And I just wrote one that I haven't released yet that's a little bit more — not political, but my take on what's going on in the world. That's been very hard for me to even speak up about, because I don't want to hurt anyone's feelings, and everything feels so incendiary; anyone could go off at any moment, about anything. So I've been like: I'm going to step back and just watch. And of course all of my songs and all of my art is commenting on everything, so I've always felt: that's enough, I don't have to hit people with what I think about things. But maybe there's a time to do it. So I'm grappling with all of that. Substack feels like the best version of social media to me, basically.

Simon: Agreed. It's a much more thoughtful environment. And I completely understand the vulnerability of that forum, the self-doubt and the questioning. But your words and your music always create a space of compassion and empathy.

Lael: Thank you for saying that. So do you write on Substack?

Simon: No. I love reading, and I'm writing an essay at the moment on the history of Australian electronic music. Part of me wonders whether that idea of thinking in public, which I think Substack is a beautiful term for, would be beneficial. But I'm so scared of it. Which is why I have such admiration for those who can articulate themselves that way. That classic Joan Didion idea: writing to find out what you think. It's a great source of clarification.

Lael: That's exactly the gift of Substack for people who like to write, but maybe don't feel like they completely know their voice yet. It's a really good space. I feel like you should definitely put that in there. Just the act of doing things like that is so beneficial, and you will come to more clarity about what you want to say, and what your perspective is. And I want to read it.

Simon: You've been writing for so many years. Is journaling still a daily practice for you?

Lael: Yeah, I've just restarted a dream journal, and then I do writing in the morning.

Simon: A beautiful ritual, and part of that process of clarification, like you were saying. I can't thank you enough for your time. The album is out, and you've just finished touring as well?

Lael: Yeah, just got back last week from Europe, actually.

Simon: I hear it went brilliantly, so congratulations. Hopefully there'll be an Australian trip at some point.

Lael: I know, we keep talking about it. The guy who I play with really wants us to go. I mean, I want to go too, but he's all bent on getting us there.

Simon: It has to happen.

Lael: Where exactly are you?

Simon: In Melbourne, in Victoria. It would be extraordinary. We're all campaigning for it down here.

Lael: Thank you so much.

Simon: Thank you again, for your time and your amazing work.

Lael: Thank you. Thanks for all the questions, and for caring.

pullQuote.text: No matter how tragic and destructive things are, we have to have the hope to keep going.
pullQuote.speaker: Lael Neale
